pages.x: Persia ruled the largest empire the world had yet seen, from Egypt to India, and with it the Greek cities on the coast of Turkey. In 499 BC those cities rebelled, and Athens sent ships to help them burn the Persian city of Sardis. King Darius crushed the revolt and swore to punish Athens.

In 490 BC a Persian army landed at Marathon, 40 km from Athens. The Athenians, helped only by little Plataea, charged at a run and drove them back to their ships. Legend says a messenger ran all the way to Athens with the news and then dropped dead, the story behind today's marathon race.

Ten years later Darius's son Xerxes came with a vast army and fleet. At the narrow pass of Thermopylae, King Leonidas of Sparta held him off for three days, until a local man showed the Persians a path around the pass. Leonidas, his 300 Spartans and the allies who stayed with them fought to the last.

Athens was abandoned and burned. But its leader Themistocles lured the Persian fleet into the narrow strait of Salamis, where its numbers counted for nothing. Xerxes watched from a throne on the shore as the Greek triremes rammed and sank his ships.

In 479 BC the Greek allies, led by Sparta, destroyed the Persian army left behind in Greece at Plataea. On the same day, it was said, a Greek fleet burned the Persian ships at Mycale. Persia never again tried to conquer Greece.

Herodotus, born in a Greek city under Persian rule, travelled widely asking people what had happened and why. His Histories, the story of these wars, earned him the name father of history. He also reports plenty of gossip, and often says when he does not believe it.

The Greek victories kept Persia out of Europe and let Athens grow into the city of democracy, theatre and philosophy. The wars were long told as freedom against tyranny, though Persia was a tolerant empire and many Greeks fought on its side.
pts: Kept the Greek cities free of Persian rule
Opened the golden age of Athens
